lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.unitTitle: Body Signals, Rest, and Fueling Meals
lessonRef.title: Correction and reflection: asking a trusted adult for help

standardsRefs: Ready for Life v1, Grade 4 Unit 4: Body Signals, Rest, and Fueling Meals
objective: Learners identify one recent moment when they noticed a body signal (hunger, thirst, stress, or tiredness) but didn't ask a trusted adult for help clearly, write a vague version and a specific two-part version (signal plus need) of what they could have said, and predict how each version would likely be received.
scenario: Sometimes a learner notices hunger, thirst, stress, or being overly tired but doesn't say anything to a trusted adult, or asks in a way that's hard to act on, like saying they don't feel good. This lesson has the learner think back to one real moment like that, then practice building a specific request they could use next time.

tasks.directions: Think back over the last week to one specific moment when you noticed a body signal (hunger, thirst, stress, or tiredness) but didn't ask a trusted adult for help with it, or asked in a way that was hard to understand.

prompts.text: Describe that moment: what signal did you notice, and what happened instead of asking clearly?

tasks.directions: For that same moment, write two versions of what you could have said: a vague version, like saying you don't feel good, and a specific version that names both the signal and what you need, like naming that your stomach feels empty and asking for something to eat soon.

prompts.text: My vague version is realistic, close to something I might actually say without thinking.
My specific version names the actual signal I noticed.
My specific version names one clear thing I need, not just a description of the problem.

tasks.directions: Compare your vague version and your specific version side by side and think through how a trusted adult would likely respond to each one if you actually said them out loud.

prompts.text: Predict how a trusted adult would probably respond to your vague version, and then to your specific version. What's different about the two predicted responses?
Name one reason the specific version is easier for another person to act on quickly.

tasks.directions: Think about a moment that might come up again this week.

prompts.text: Write the specific two-part request (signal plus need) you plan to actually use next time you notice hunger, thirst, stress, or tiredness, and explain why you chose that wording.

remediation: If a learner's 'specific' version still stays vague, like just saying they need help with no named signal or need, reteach with a two-blank sentence frame ('I'm noticing ___, and I need ___') and have the learner fill in the blanks for three different practice signals before returning to their own moment.
extension: Have the learner practice saying their specific two-part request out loud to a trusted adult in a calm moment, not during an actual signal, and write down what the adult said back.
